authors.affiliation: Packaging Technology Division, Industrial Technology Development Institute (DOST-ITDI), Department of Science and Technology

papers.title: AST/ALT Ratio as a Diagnostic Biomarker for Hepatocellular Carcinoma (HCC) in a Filipino Population and The Potential of AI Integration for Early Diagnosis
papers.abstract: Hepatocellular carcinoma remains one of the predominant malignancies, especially in Asian populations, with its incidence rising with age. Current diagnostic methods are invasive, limited in diagnostic sensitivity, and are not integrated into routine laboratory screenings. Furthermore, it can pose a significant economic barrier for developing countries like the Philippines. Therefore, this study aims to assess the predictive accuracy of Aspartate aminotransferase/Alanine Transaminase ratio and Artificial Intelligence-driven models as a preliminary diagnostic biomarker for early hepatocellular carcinoma detection in Filipino patients. Data analysis from a previously reported 2025 Filipino clinical cohort revealed highly statistically significant elevations in enzyme levels (p < 0.0001), resulting in a shift in median ratios from 0.89 in control groups to 1.18 in hepatocellular carcinoma patients. These validated thresholds were applied in a stratification-based approach using a spreadsheet tool to categorize patient risk. The results of this study are expected to demonstrate how routine laboratory markers can be used for risk stratification and early diagnosis of hepatocellular carcinoma. While this is based on a single previously reported cohort and has not been validated in a larger population, it establishes a functional framework for using accessible enzyme ratios as a guide for early detection. This approach seeks to improve patient outcomes through timely diagnosis and early-action strategies, allowing prevention and/or reducing the long-term clinical and economic burden of advanced malignancy.

keynote.speaker: Dr. Feorillo Petronillo DEMETERIO III
keynote.title: Beyond Efficiency: Harnessing Generative AI for Research Excellence in Philippine HEIs
keynote.bio: Dr. Feorillo A. Demeterio III is a Distinguished Full Professor of the Department of Filipino, College of Liberal Arts, De La Salle University, and Head of the Matter and Memory Research Laboratory. He has extensive experience in research administration, capacity building, and scholarly mentoring, being the Executive Director of the University's Research and Grants Management Office for more than a decade now. In recent years, Dr. Demeterio has developed particular expertise in AI-assisted research mentoring, especially in guiding faculty members, graduate students, and researchers in the strategic use of generative AI across different stages of the research process. His mentoring work covers the development and refinement of research titles and problems, systematic and scoping literature reviews, conceptual and theoretical frameworks, research design, qualitative and quantitative analysis, article extraction, results-and-discussion writing, journal targeting, and manuscript development. He has designed and facilitated numerous workshops and writeshops on AI-assisted research and scholarly publication. Dr. Demeterio is the author or co-author of several books and more than a hundred scholarly articles in hermeneutics, cultural studies, Philippine studies, and Filipino philosophy. He has held visiting research appointments in Washington, D.C., and Hong Kong, and is a co-founder of the Andrew Gonzalez Philippine Citation Index.
keynote.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence is rapidly transforming research from a largely individual and sequential process into a more interactive, iterative, and computationally augmented form of knowledge production. This keynote argues that the value of generative AI for Philippine higher education institutions extends far beyond efficiency and automation. Properly integrated, generative AI can strengthen research excellence by supporting researchers across the research cycle—from problem formulation, literature searching and synthesis, conceptual and theoretical framing, research design, data analysis, interpretation, visualization, and scholarly writing to publication preparation. It can likewise enhance research mentoring by enabling more sustained feedback, scaffolding methodological reasoning, diagnosing weaknesses in manuscripts, and helping mentors guide larger and more diverse groups of researchers. The presentation further examines how generative AI is reshaping the research ecosystem by changing expectations regarding researcher competencies, mentoring practices, publication workflows, institutional research support, and research governance. It argues that Philippine HEIs must move from defensive or purely regulatory responses toward deliberate institutional adaptation. This requires developing AI literacy, ethical and transparent research practices, appropriate governance frameworks, and AI-assisted research mentoring systems. The central challenge is therefore not whether Philippine HEIs should use generative AI, but how they can harness it responsibly to expand research capacity, improve scholarly quality, and strengthen their participation in global knowledge production.

papers.title: Gender-Inclusive Lessons in Purposive Communication
papers.abstract: Gender inclusivity in teacher education is an essential component in creating equitable and empowering learning environments for students with diverse gender identities and experiences. Despite existing policies and frameworks that promote gender inclusivity, gaps remain in the implementation of gender-inclusive practices in English Language Teaching (ELT) classrooms. Guided by Queer Pedagogy and Dick and Carey's instructional design model, this study explored gender-inclusive ELT practices in Purposive Communication classes in three higher education institutions in Goa, Camarines Sur across instructional preparation, materials, delivery, interaction, and assessment. It also sought to develop gender-inclusive lesson exemplars that could support inclusive teaching practices. Using a descriptive-developmental research design, the study employed document analysis, classroom observations, instructor interviews, and expert validation. The developed lesson exemplars underwent expert evaluation and yielded a 9.21 rating, which translates to high compliance. Findings revealed that existing ELT practices demonstrated awareness of gender inclusivity but often reflected surface-level implementation. Current practices often reflect surface-level inclusion, revealing a gap between policy and classroom implementation. The study concludes that gender-inclusive instruction must be intentional, systematic, and critically grounded. It recommends integrating explicit gender-inclusive outcomes in syllabi, enhancing instructional materials, strengthening inclusive classroom interaction and assessment, and providing continuous teacher training to support sustainable implementation of gender-inclusive practices. Finally, the study recommends the institutionalization of gender inclusivity through explicit integration in instruction, course outcomes, materials, and structured classroom engagement and assessment. This underscores the need for systemic support and continuous professional development in promoting gender inclusivity in ELT classrooms.

papers.title: Reimagining Philippine Education for Human Flourishing: Beyond Access and Employability
papers.abstract: Philippines continues to face learning crisis characterized by poor educational outcomes and persistent inequalities, particularly among learners from remote and economically disadvantaged communities. Although existing policies have improved and expanded free access to education, many students remain unable to go to school because of poverty, geographical conditions, and other constraints that extend beyond the four corners of the classroom. The paper examines whether there is a need to reimagine the educational system and argues that reforms must extend beyond access-based solutions towards a model that is philosophically grounded. Through a philosophical-analytical approach, the study examines the Philippine education through the lens of Aristotle's concept of Eudaimonia (human flourishing). It draws on literature related to Shanti Bhavan Residential School in India, a model that tries to address socioeconomic barriers that often prevent children from succeeding in school. The paper examines three interconnected issues: the limits of access-based educational reforms; the ethical and cultural challenges of residential schooling in the Philippine setting; and the distinction between schooling and genuine education. The analysis argues that free education is insufficient when learners face interconnected setbacks such as malnutrition, lack of transportation, unsafe housing. It further suggests that a culturally sensitive residential schooling may help address these barriers, and finally, the paper asserts that education should not be viewed merely for economic productivity, rather should nurture critical thinking, moral judgment, creativity, and sense of responsibility toward others. Ultimately, the paper concludes that a reimagined Philippine educational system should be grounded in Aristotle's concept of Eudaimonia, where education aims not only at economic advancement but also at the cultivation of fully flourishing human beings.

papers.title: Typologies of Sustainable AI Integration: Profiling Continuous Professional Adoption and Socio-Cultural Adaptability among Prospective Teachers Through the Lens of Industry 4.0
papers.abstract: The rapid paradigm shift driven by Industry 4.0 demands a resilient workforce of educators capable of navigating advanced technological ecosystems. In teacher education, this transition requires dual imperative competence. These are continuous professional AI adoption (CPAIA) as well as Socio-Cultural and Contextual Adaptability (SCCA). This study investigates the unobserved heterogeneous mindsets of prospective teachers aligned with DigCompEdu framework. Methodology: A cross-sectional quantitative research design was employed, utilizing a sample of 360 prospective teachers from teacher education institutions in Northeast India. Data were gathered using a validated psychometric scale capturing two core dimensions these were CPAIA (6 items) and SCCA (6 items), rated on a 5-point Likert scale. Given the limitations of traditional central-tendency metrics or cluster analysis in capturing hidden subgroups, Latent Profile Analysis (LPA), a person-centeric model-based approach was executed to extract distinct behavioural typologies. Model fit was evaluated using information criteria (AIC, BIC, SABIC) and classification precision (entropy) and class prevalence (sample distribution). Findings: The Latent Profile Analysis demonstrated that a 3-profile model yielded the optimal statistical fit with the lowest Bayesian Information Criterion (BIC- 6508) and high entropy (.98). These extracted typologies revealed three distinct configurations. These were Tech-Centric Adopters (10.3%) Context-Driven Adaptors (9.7%) Holistically Resilient Educators (80%). Conclusion: The study concludes that prospective teachers do not possess a homogeneity within given construct. The identified typologies underscore the critical need for teacher training frameworks to move away from one size fit for all with digital literacy policies. Findings advocated for contextualized, inclusive and sustainable AI capacity-building modules to address this heterogeneity among prospective teachers.

authors.name: Anshu Chandra
authors.affiliation: Department of Teacher Education, Nagaland University, Kohima Campus, Nagaland

papers.title: Academic Integrity in Generative AI Use among Pre-Service Teachers: A Systematic Review
papers.abstract: Introduction. The growing use of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) in teacher education has changed how preservice teachers complete academic work, raising concerns about academic integrity, authorship, and ethical AI use. As future educators, preservice teachers must balance GenAI's pedagogical benefits with the responsibility to model ethical technology use. This systematic review examined how preservice teachers use generative AI academically and the strategies they employ to maintain academic integrity. Methodology. This study used a systematic review guided by the PRISMA framework. Literature published between January 2023 and June 2026 was searched across ERIC, Google Scholar, and Philippine e-Journals using predefined Boolean strings. Studies were screened using the Population–Interest–Context (PICo) framework and evaluated through a four-point rigor checklist. Twenty-seven peer-reviewed empirical studies met inclusion criteria and underwent qualitative thematic synthesis. Findings. Preservice teachers primarily use generative AI for lesson planning, instructional material development, assessment design, academic writing, research support, literature synthesis, and administrative productivity. To uphold academic integrity, they disclose AI assistance transparently, cite AI-generated content properly, critically verify AI outputs against credible sources, follow institutional policies, and engage in reflective ethical decision-making. However, findings also reveal variability in institutional AI guidelines and AI literacy levels, underscoring the continuing need for clearer policy frameworks and ethics education within teacher preparation programs. Conclusions. Generative AI has become an important academic support tool for preservice teachers, but responsible use depends on integrating AI literacy, ethical reasoning, and institutional guidance. Teacher education institutions should strengthen AI governance through explicit policies, ethics-focused instruction, and authentic assessment practices that encourage responsible use while preserving academic integrity. Future longitudinal research is recommended to examine how preservice teachers' ethical AI practices evolve as they transition into the profession.

papers.title: Navigating the Dual Life: A Mixed Methods Analysis of the Agonies and Triumphs of Working College Students in a State University
papers.abstract: In the contemporary Philippine higher education landscape, student employment has shifted from a voluntary pursuit to a socio-economic necessity. This study investigated the dualistic experiences of working students in a State University, conceptualized through the "Agony" of structural constraints and the "Triumph" of psychological resilience. Utilizing a sequential explanatory mixed-methods design (quanti-quali), the research first surveyed 200 working students using the Maslach Burnout Inventory-General Survey (MBI-GS). Quantitative results revealed a moderate to high level of Emotional Exhaustion (M \= 3.85), which significantly correlated with academic burnout; however, Academic Efficacy scores remained paradoxically robust (M \= 4.10), showing a strong positive correlation with GPA (r \= 0.52, p < .01). The subsequent qualitative phase, involving semi-structured interviews with 15 purposively selected participants, employed Hobfoll's Conservation of Resources (COR) Theory to explain this resilience. Five core themes emerged: (1) The Agony of Time Poverty, (2) Social Displacement and Double-Consciousness, (3) The Triumph of Hyper-Efficiency, (4) Cognitive Flexibility through a "Secondary Curriculum," and (5) The Reconstruction of Identity via Financial Agency. The integration of findings suggests that while work intensity poses physiological risks, it simultaneously acts as a crucible for developing professional maturity, grit, and self-determination. The study concludes that working students are "Resilient Practitioners" whose academic success is tempered by, rather than achieved despite, their labor. Recommendations include the adoption of compassionate pedagogy, inclusive scheduling, and the establishment of university "Resilience Hubs" to mitigate structural agonies.

keynote.speaker: Dr. Dexter DELA CRUZ
keynote.title: From coral reproduction to reef recovery: innovative technologies for large-scale coral restoration
keynote.bio: Dr Dexter dela Cruz is a marine scientist and coral reef restoration researcher with more than 20 years of research experience. His research focuses on coral reproduction, larval ecology, conservation, and the development of scalable technologies for restoring degraded coral reef ecosystems. Dr. dela Cruz earned his Bachelor's degree in Biology, from the Pamantasan ng Lungsod ng Maynila and pursued his Master's degree in Marine Science at the Marine Science Institute (MSI), University of the Philippines Diliman. During his Master's, he was a recipient of research scholarships from the Global Environment Facility (GEF)–World Bank and the European Union. At MSI, he was fortunate to be trained under the late National Scientist Dr. Edgardo D. Gomez, founder of the Marine Science Institute and one of the pioneers of marine science and coral reef conservation in the Philippines. During his time at the University of the Philippines, he worked on a range of international and government-funded research projects gaining extensive field and research experience across Philippine coral reef ecosystems. This formative experience provided the foundation for his continuing work in coral reef research and restoration. He later completed his PhD in Marine Biology at Southern Cross University, Australia, as a recipient of the prestigious John Allwright Fellowship of the Australian Centre for International Agricultural Research (ACIAR), Australia Awards. Dr. dela Cruz has been leading the development of groundbreaking coral reef restoration techniques applied in the Philippines, Australia, and other parts of the world to restore degraded reefs and enhance their resilience to climate change. Working with Distinguished Professor Peter Harrison of Southern Cross University, his research has contributed to scientific evidence demonstrating that reseeding degraded reefs with microscopic coral larvae can successfully re-establish viable coral populations, with restored corals reaching reproductive maturity and spawning within two years of seeding. Importantly, restoration sites have also shown increasing fish abundance, demonstrating the broader ecological benefits of coral restoration beyond the recovery of coral populations. His coral restoration research has also extended to international reef systems in Indonesia, Kenya, Madagascar, and the Maldives, contributing to the application and evaluation of restoration approaches across diverse geographical and environmental settings. Building on this body of work, in 2027 he will co-lead the largest coral reef restoration project in the Philippines, funded jointly by the Australian Government and the Philippine Department of Science and Technology (DOST), further advancing the application of scalable coral restoration technologies at a national level. Dr. dela Cruz has published extensively in peer-reviewed international scientific journals, contributing to the fields of coral reproduction, larval ecology, coral reef restoration, and climate resilience. His research has received more than 900 citations and an h-index of 12 on Google Scholar, reflecting the international impact of his scientific contributions. His contributions to marine science and coral reef restoration have received several prestigious recognitions. He was named Australia Awards Alumnus of the Year in 2023, followed by Southern Cross University International Alumnus of the Year in 2024. In 2024, he also received the Mid-Career Research Excellence Award from Southern Cross University, recognizing his research achievements and sustained contribution to marine science and coral reef restoration. His career reflects a longstanding commitment to combining scientific research and innovation, capacity building, and field-based restoration to build resilient and future-ready coral reef ecosystems.
keynote.abstract: Coral reefs are among the most biologically diverse and valuable ecosystems on Earth, supporting fisheries, coastal protection, tourism, food security, and the livelihoods and well-being of hundreds of millions of people worldwide. They also provide essential ecological functions that sustain biodiversity and coastal communities, particularly across tropical developing regions. Yet these ecosystems are experiencing unprecedented declines as climate change, marine heatwaves, ocean acidification, pollution, overfishing, sedimentation, and coastal development increasingly exceed their capacity for natural recovery. The urgent challenge is therefore not only to conserve remaining coral reefs, but also to develop restoration approaches capable of rebuilding functional, resilient, future-ready, and self-sustaining reef communities at meaningful spatial scales. Coral larval enhancement technology offers a fundamentally different pathway by harnessing mass spawning to produce millions of sexually derived, genetically diverse corals and introducing them into degraded reef habitats. Recent technological and innovative advances are rapidly expanding the potential scale of this approach. This presentation brings together these researches with long-term restoration outcomes tracing the pathway from coral sexual reproduction and in situ larval culture to larval deployment, coral community establishment, and reef recovery.

papers.title: Design and Simulation of a Small-Scale Fresnel Lens Solar Concentrated Biochar System for Agri-Waste Utilization
papers.abstract: This study focuses on the design, simulation, and technical evaluation of a small-scale, hybrid solar-assisted biochar processor tailored for smallholder farmers in off-grid rural areas. The system integrates a Fresnel lens solar concentrator guided by an ESP32 microcontroller for automatic sun-tracking, auxiliary heating, and a ceramic fiber-insulated pyrolysis chamber to convert local agricultural waste into value-added biochar. The processor has a 2 kg dry biomass capacity per batch and produces biochar intended for soil amendment applications to improve soil quality and agricultural productivity. A Raspberry Pi with a NoIR camera provides visual process monitoring, while physicochemical analyses evaluate system performance across various feedstocks, including coconut husk, rice husk, sawdust, and banana leaves. Experimental results demonstrate that the system consistently achieves effective operating temperatures between 400–600 °C, successfully carbonizing all tested biomass types. Laboratory analysis confirmed that the resulting biochar exhibited favorable physicochemical properties, such as neutral to strongly alkaline pH and stable fixed carbon content. Among the feedstocks, rice husk yielded the most uniform and stable biochar, banana leaves carbonized the fastest (within 30–60 minutes) due to high surface area, and sawdust produced the highest fixed carbon content despite having the slowest carbonization rate. While this prototype successfully validates the mechanical and thermal integration of solar-driven pyrolysis, actual testing revealed operational constraints. Structural vibrations from the agitator, uneven thermal distribution, minor exhaust leakage, and a semi-manual roller blind mechanism limited overall efficiency. Future refinements focusing on structural dynamics, dual-axis solar tracking, full automation, and optimized heating coil geometry are recommended to enhance reliability and scalability for sustainable rural agriculture.

authors.name: Antipuesto Myke Edward
authors.affiliation: Rhienyel V. Busto, Brylle Vincent C. Mojica, Jenny S. Noveno, Johanna Marie M. Perocho, Justin Ladz P. Vicedo ( Philippines)

papers.title: Utilizing the Phyphox Application for Replicable Modal Analysis: A Pedestrian Serviceability Assessment of the Baler Zibali Hanging Bridge in a Remote Coastal Zone
papers.abstract: Long-span pedestrian suspension bridges in remote coastal environments face unique structural challenges due to inherent flexibility and low dynamic stiffness. The Baler Zibali Hanging Bridge, characterized by its 115-meter span and significant sag, is particularly susceptible to Serviceability Limit State issues resulting from pedestrian-induced vibrations. This study evaluates the structure's dynamic response using a "citizen sensing" methodology, employing smartphone-integrated triaxial Micro-Electro-Mechanical System (MEMS) accelerometers and the Phyphox application as low-cost sensors. Raw time-history acceleration data were processed in MATLAB using Fast Fourier Transform and Power Spectral Density functions to isolate fundamental modal frequencies across multiple bridge nodes. The extracted vertical frequencies of 0.585 Hz and 1.074 Hz remain safely below the critical 1.6 Hz to 4.5 Hz resonance window typically associated with pedestrian footfall excitation. Conversely, the recorded lateral fundamental frequencies of 0.585 Hz, 0.830 Hz, and 1.611 Hz fall within highly sensitive bands. Specifically, the 0.585 Hz and 0.830 Hz modes are situated within the 0.50–1.20 Hz transverse frequency range, making the 115m span exceptionally prone to the "lock-in" effect. In this state, pedestrians synchronize their gait with the bridge's sway, leading to resonant forces that impair user comfort and balance. Field observations corroborated these findings, identifying that an occupancy density of exactly five pedestrians triggers the maximum lateral response. Consequently, the study validates a strict 5-pedestrian occupancy limit to maintain structural serviceability. This research demonstrates that high-resolution modal analysis via low-cost mobile hardware is a viable alternative to complex numerical modeling, establishing a replicable framework for data-driven infrastructure management in remote coastal regions.

papers.title: HYAHUB: An Integrated Water Hyacinth Processing and Livelihood Community for a Centralized Hub Towards Sustainable Tourism
papers.abstract: Water hyacinth, a perennial and invasive aquatic plant, rapidly forms dense colonies spreading through rivers and lakes, disrupting freshwater biodiversity and obstructing waterways affecting fishing, river transport, damage bridges, and clog dams. Despite its negative impacts, it offers various potentials and innovations transforming it into a sustainable product and livelihood opportunities which can help to manage and mitigate its excessive volume. However, existing government support and community facilities operate with fragmented systems and equipment, resulting in having a significant opportunity to establish a centralized and integrated facility that can streamline processing, support livelihood development, and maximize the plant's potential. The main objective of this study is to explore and identify the existing conditions, practices and limitations of water hyacinth facilities and livelihood communities to serve as a guide in designing a centralized and integrated hub for water hyacinth towards sustainable tourism, to evaluate its potential contributions in the environment, society and its economic development. The data gathered utilized qualitative research through exploratory research design by employing observation and semi-structured interviews, where it is analyzed through thematic analysis. Analysis revealed water hyacinth's persistent challenges and to mitigate its volume, facilities such as Cardona Water Hyacinth Primary Processing Center, Tapayan Water Hyacinth Processing Facility and Better Pililla Women's Multi-Purpose Cooperative (PiLILYA Handicrafts) utilize it to be used as a byproduct. However, data gathered indicated that while these facilities possess notable strengths, they also face operational gaps and limitations that restrict its full potential. Respondents expressed strong interest in establishing a centralized and integrated hub that connects processing, various production of product, training, and marketing. The findings provide a foundational framework and suggest that such hubs can enhance the environmental management, support livelihood community, promote sustainable tourism, and strengthen circular bioeconomy by transforming water hyacinth from a burden into a valuable resource.

papers.title: Lived Experiences of Filipino Barangay Captains In Disaster Risk Reduction Management: A Phenomenological Study
papers.abstract: Community resilience and safety are vital foundations for sustainable development in the Philippines. At the barangay level, structured approaches play a crucial role in strengthening preparedness and response capacities. Barangay captains play a vital role in overseeing local disaster preparedness, coordinating response efforts, and maintaining order during emergencies. However, limited studies have explored their lived experiences in implementing Disaster Risk Reduction and Management (DRRM) at the grassroots level. This study aimed to explore the lived experiences of barangay captains in selected flood-prone barangays, focusing on their roles, challenges, decision-making, and resilience in managing disaster situations. The study utilized a qualitative phenomenological design to understand the participants' experiences. Participants were selected from five barangay captains in one of the municipalities of Misamis Occidental, Philippines. Data were collected through semi-structured interviews and analyzed using Moustakas' (1994) phenomenological analysis. The findings revealed five major themes: (1) leadership responsibility and moral accountability; (2) emotional impact of fear and stress; (3) disaster preparedness, monitoring, and early warning processes; (4) operational response and community safety measures; and (5) leadership decision-making. Their experiences emphasized the importance of preparedness, early warning systems, and collaboration with local government units and community members. It is recommended that barangay-level DRRM be strengthened through leadership training, psychosocial support, and community participation to build resilient grassroots governance.

papers.title: Effects of Land Reclamation on Small-Scale Fisheries in Manila Bay Coastal Communities of Parañaque and Navotas
papers.abstract: Coastal land reclamation has become a dominant urban development strategy in Metro Manila, yet its socio-environmental impacts on small-scale fishing communities remain unevenly understood. Drawing on political ecology as a theoretical foundation, this study examines land reclamation as both a physical transformation of coastal space and a process shaped by unequal power relations, competing claims over Manila Bay, and uneven access to marine resources. In the cities of Navotas and Parañaque, reclamation has increasingly restricted access to fishing and mussel farming areas, raising concerns over livelihood disruption among coastal communities dependent on fisheries. This study examined how fisherfolk in both sites perceived and experienced reclamation-driven changes. A qualitative research design was employed, involving 20 purposively selected participants, with 10 participants from each site, who participated in semi-structured interviews. Data were analyzed using Braun and Clarke's Reflexive Thematic Analysis. Findings revealed five cross-cutting themes: fishing routines, finances and resources, government response, perceptions and emotions, and environmental impacts. Site-specific themes also emerged. In Navotas, where reclamation projects remain ongoing, fisherfolk emphasized coping mechanisms shaped by both anticipated and already experienced impacts. In contrast, fisherfolk in Parañaque, where reclamation-related infrastructure has already been completed, highlighted how private sector activities have intensified environmental degradation and livelihood disruption. Comparative analysis indicates that the impacts of reclamation are stage-dependent, with ongoing and completed projects producing distinct but interconnected forms of uncertainty, displacement, and livelihood vulnerability. The study conceptualizes land reclamation as a socio-ecological restructuring process that generates uneven livelihood vulnerabilities among coastal communities. It highlights the need for participatory and accountable coastal governance that actively involves fisherfolk in reclamation-related decision-making, alongside transparent communication, stronger accountability mechanisms, and fair support systems for affected coastal communities.

keynote.speaker: Dr. Michael Joseph DINO
keynote.title: Hybrid Artificial Intelligence for Resilient and Inclusive Health Communities

papers.title: Development of a Data-Driven Predictive Framework for Early Heart Disease Detection Using Machine Learning: A Comparative Analysis Across KDD, DDDM, Health Informatics, and Statistical Learning Theory Frameworks
papers.abstract: Cardiovascular disease (CVD) remains the leading global cause of mortality, a challenge exacerbated by the predictive limitations of traditional linear risk models which fail to account for complex, non-linear interactions in patient data. This study engineered a robust data-driven predictive framework for early heart disease detection by rigorously integrating the Knowledge Discovery in Databases (KDD) process with the clinical focus of the Data-Driven Decision-Making (DDDM) framework. Six machine learning (ML) algorithms, including Logistic Regression (LR), Support Vector Machine (SVM), Linear Discriminant Analysis (LDA), Decision Trees (DT), Neural Networks (NN), and Random Forest (RF), were comparatively evaluated on the benchmark Cleveland Heart Disease dataset via stratified k-fold cross-validation. All models demonstrated strong discriminatory power, with the highly interpretable Logistic Regression achieving a specificity of 88.41% and sensitivity of 80.58%, supported by a statistically significant McFadden R-squared. Crucially, feature importance analysis consistently identified structural and genetic indicators—specifically Fluoroscopy results (ca) (number of calcified vessels) and Thalassemia—as the two most dominant predictors of CVD risk. Conversely, conventional metabolic markers like Serum Cholesterol and Fasting Blood Sugar exhibited negligible predictive influence. This research validates the integrated ML framework as a powerful, transparent instrument for proactive cardiovascular risk assessment, advocating for a crucial clinical paradigm shift toward structural and functional diagnostics.

authors.name: Jared Lomibao
authors.affiliation: University of the Philippines Los Baños

papers.title: Experiences and Challenges of PT Interns from a Local University in Transitioning from Classroom to Clinical Environment: A Qualitative Study
papers.abstract: The transition from classroom learning to clinical internship is a significant stage in physical therapy education, as it allows students to apply their knowledge and skills in actual healthcare settings. However, this transition is often accompanied by various academic, emotional, and professional challenges that may affect interns' learning experiences and adaptation to clinical practice. This study aimed to explore the experiences, challenges, and perceived academic preparation gaps of Physical Therapy (PT) interns from a local university during their transition to clinical internship. Guided by Schlossberg's Transition Theory, specifically the 4S Model (Situation, Self, Support, and Strategies), the study examined how interns navigated and adapted to the demands of the clinical environment. A descriptive qualitative research design was utilized, involving nine (9) PT interns selected through purposive sampling. Data were collected through three (3) semi-structured focus group discussions and analyzed using thematic and content analysis to identify recurring patterns and themes. Findings revealed that interns encountered challenges related to institutional policies and practices, theory-practice gaps, role ambiguity, and differences between classroom learning and clinical realities. Participants reported experiencing mixed emotions, including anxiety, uncertainty, and excitement, while facing difficulties such as inconsistent supervision, communication barriers, workload expectations, and limited opportunities for clinical competency development. Despite these challenges, support from peers, family members, patients, and clinical staff contributed to a smoother transition. Interns also utilized coping strategies such as maintaining a positive mindset, engaging in proactive learning, seeking guidance, and adapting to new situations. Overall, the findings highlight the importance of adequate preparation, support systems, and adaptive strategies in facilitating a successful transition from academic training to clinical practice.

papers.title: Pagtatandok of the Ilocanos: Sustaining traditional way of treating animal bites in Anao, Tarlac
papers.abstract: Asia has been the bastion of traditional medicines and treatment. China has Traditional Chinese Medicines (TMC), India has Ayurveda, Thailand has Traditional Thai Medicine (TTM), Philippines has Traditional Filipino Medicine (TFM) which is rooted from indigenous folklore, cultural practices and beliefs, herbalism, and spiritual healing. Nursing and provision of health care in the Philippines could be traced back during the intuitive period of the 6th century when nursing practice was instinctive, untaught and without conscious reasoning. Modern ways of medication are now provided. This study investigates its continued existence of pagtatandok, the traditional way of treating animal bites infected with rabies from the human body through suction methods and materials by the Ilocanos. Triangulation method was used to gather and validate data. The narratives of four (5) Ilocano practitioners of pagtatandok in Anao, Tarlac were utilized to determine the continued existence of the traditional way of treating animal bites infected with rabies. Pakikipagkuwentuhan was done to get the experiences of the patients who sought pagtatandok after being bitten by rabid animals. Survey Questionnaires were distributed to people who were not yet bitten by rabies-infected animals but will seek pagtatandok. Anchored in Madeleine Leininger's Culture Care Theory, this paper argued that nursing care must fit with individual group's, or institution's cultural values, beliefs, and lifeways”. The study revealed that pagtatandok is still existent because of psychological, sociological, and economic reasons. Pagtatandok as a way of treating animal bites infected with rabies, must not be eradicated but should be respected, improved, and validated. The mangngag-agas who perform pagtatandok are not societal enemies but are partners of the society. This study calles for fusion of modern nursing intervention and the indigenous cultural practice as a response to Sustainable Development Goal #3 (Health and Well-Being). Key terms: Traditional medicine; rabies; pagtatandok; mangngag-agas; animal bite

papers.title: Unveiling the Shadows: Exploring Microaggression Towards People of Diverse Sogiesc in Basc as a Basis For Gender-Responsive Policy
papers.abstract: People of diverse Sexual Orientation, Gender Identity and Expression, and Sex Characteristics (SOGIESC), better known as the LGBTQ community, were constantly under the shadows of microaggression. It may be obvious or hidden in day-to-day interactions and undetectable in conversations. Moreover, it can be manifested through comments, actions, or behavior that conveys a negative message to a specific individual or a group. This study aimed to explore the lived experiences of LGBTQ students and staff at Bulacan Agricultural State College (BASC) who experienced microaggressions. Eighteen (18) participants were interviewed following a hermeneutic phenomenological research design. Results revealed substantial emergent themes, namely: 1. Hidden Harms, 2. Silenced Voices, 3. Institutional Walls, 4. Resilience and Resistance. These themes were vital in formulating gender-responsive policy and interventions, which in turn may be of great importance in promoting a gender-inclusive and safe space for the people of diverse SOGIESC in BASC. Furthermore, this study supports the effort to promote good health and well-being (SDG 3), eliminate discrimination in education (SDG 4), end all forms of discrimination against women, girls, and all genders (SDG 5), and foster inclusion (SDG 10).

keynote.speaker: Prof. Dr. Aldrin BONTO
keynote.title: Exploring Food Structure and Functionalities: Unveiling Insights Through Material Science Perspectives
keynote.abstract: Food matrices are multiscale, heterogeneous materials whose physicochemical and functional properties emerge from complex interactions among biopolymers, water, micronutrients, and processing-induced structural transformations. This presentation examines food systems through a material science framework, focusing on structure–property–function relationships across molecular, microstructural, and macroscopic scales. Using cereal grains, starch-rich matrices, plant-derived flours, and polysaccharide-based materials as representative systems, the effects of emerging and conventional processing strategies, including ultrasonication, atmospheric cold plasma, germination, and fortification, on material organization and functionality are discussed. Particular attention is given to changes in surface characteristics, crystallinity, molecular interactions, thermal transitions, rheological behavior, hydration, texture, and nutrient accessibility. Complementary characterization using Fourier-transform infrared spectroscopy, X-ray diffraction, microscopy, differential scanning calorimetry, thermogravimetric analysis, particle and surface characterization, and multivariate chemometric approaches enables mechanistic interpretation of processing-induced transformations. The discussion further extends material science concepts toward engineered starch-based systems, highlighting how controlled structural modification can tailor mechanical and functional performance. This materials-driven approach provides a mechanistic platform for linking processing, structure, and functionality, supporting the rational design of next-generation food materials with improved nutritional and sustainability attributes.

papers.title: Enabling Circular Economy Practices in Sustainable Construction through Digital Technologies: A PRISMA-Based Systematic Literature Review and Conceptual Framework
papers.abstract: The construction sector remains one of the most resource-intensive industries globally, accounting for approximately 40% of raw material consumption and 30% of total solid waste generation, underscoring the urgent need for transformative approaches to resource governance in the built environment. This study presents a Bibliometric-Systematic Literature Review (B-SLR) examining how digital technologies enable Circular Economy (CE) practices in sustainable construction, following the PRISMA 2020 guidelines across four databases — Scopus, Web of Science, IEEE Xplore, and ScienceDirect. From an initial pool of 3,325 records, 87 peer-reviewed studies published between 2015 and 2025 were included in the final synthesis following rigorous deduplication, title-abstract screening, full-text eligibility assessment, and quality appraisal. Bibliometric analysis revealed a compound annual growth rate of 22.4% in publication output, confirming the rapid emergence and institutionalisation of CE–digital integration as a recognised research domain. Co-keyword clustering identified five thematic clusters — BIM-enabled lifecycle management, IoT-based material tracking, AI-driven waste optimisation, blockchain-secured material traceability, and digital twin-based systemic integration — collectively accounting for 87 included studies across a structured knowledge network. A three-tier key variable framework was developed, distinguishing foundational enablers, operational drivers, and sustainability outcome indicators, moderated by organisational digital maturity, project scale, supply chain integration depth, and governance context. These findings were synthesised into the proposed Digital-Circular Built Environment Framework (D-CBEF), a theoretically grounded conceptual model integrating the Technology–Organisation–Environment framework, Socio-Technical Systems theory, and Urban Metabolism literature. The D-CBEF offers a structured, empirically derived roadmap for researchers, practitioners, and policymakers seeking to accelerate CE transitions in the built environment through strategic digital technology deployment.

papers.title: Development and Simulation-Based Validation of a Digital Twin-Driven Predictive Maintenance Framework for Electric Ground Support Equipment (e-GSE) in Airports
papers.abstract: Introduction: The increasing adoption of Electric Ground Support Equipment (e-GSE) in airports supports sustainability initiatives by reducing carbon emissions and improving operational efficiency. However, unexpected equipment failures, battery degradation, and maintenance inefficiencies continue to affect e-GSE reliability and availability. This study developed and validated a Digital Twin-Driven Predictive Maintenance Framework to support proactive maintenance decision-making and improve airport ground support operations. Methodology: The study employed a Design Science Research methodology with simulation-based validation. A framework integrating virtual asset representation, condition monitoring, predictive analytics, failure forecasting, and maintenance decision-support mechanisms was developed based on literature from Digital Twin technology, predictive maintenance, reliability engineering, and airport asset management. A comparative simulation involving 20 e-GSE units over a one-year operational period was conducted to evaluate the proposed framework against a traditional maintenance approach. Performance was assessed using equipment availability, failure frequency, downtime, and maintenance interventions. Results: Simulation results demonstrated that the Digital Twin framework achieved an average equipment availability of 99.76% compared with 99.17% under traditional maintenance. Equipment failures decreased from 364 to 58 occurrences, while downtime was reduced from 1,456 hours to 414 hours. The framework executed 91 predictive maintenance actions, enabling proactive interventions before equipment failures occurred. Conclusion: The proposed framework significantly improved reliability, availability, and maintenance efficiency of airport e-GSE operations. The findings highlight the potential of Digital Twin-enabled predictive maintenance to support intelligent, resilient, and sustainable airport operations aligned with Industry 4.0 and smart airport initiatives.

papers.title: Citizenship Education in the Age of Inclusive AI: Integrating Sociological Frameworks for Educational and Social Transformation
papers.abstract: Despite the transformative potential of higher education, Philippine public institutions often operate as social fields in which socioeconomic inequalities are reproduced rather than reduced. Drawing on Pierre Bourdieu's theory of social reproduction and Michael Apple's critique of the political role of education, this study examines how higher education can simultaneously sustain dominant social structures while providing opportunities for dialogue and dissent. Although citizenship education seeks to cultivate informed, engaged, and socially responsible citizens, its transformative potential is often constrained by students' unequal access to economic, cultural, social, and symbolic capital. As a result, citizenship education may inadvertently reinforce a hidden curriculum that privileges labor market readiness and economic productivity over critical citizenship and democratic participation. Against this backdrop, this study qualitatively explores how higher education can move beyond workforce preparation and foster critical citizenship and meaningful social transformation. It specifically investigates the potential of Artificial Intelligence (AI) and technological innovation not merely as an apparatus for instructional efficiency, but as inclusive pedagogical mechanisms capable of reducing educational inequalities. By expanding equitable access to learning resources, supporting critical inquiry, and democratizing forms of cultural and symbolic capital essential for civic engagement, AI can help address barriers that limit students' participation in democratic life. The findings suggest that inclusive and socially responsive AI initiatives can challenge existing hegemonic structures and contribute to a more equitable, democratic, and transformative model of higher education in the Philippines.

papers.title: Temporal Analysis on Verb Tense, Narrative Viewpoint, Immediacy Perception, and Character Identification in Literary Reading
papers.abstract: Literary works as artefacts reflect the times and social context in which they are produced. Actively reading literature, questioning the texts, and identifying themes are the cornerstone of literary education and critical thinking. This study dwells into a comprehensive exploration of how verb tense and narrative perspective correlate with readers' sense of immediacy and character identity in Contemporary Literature. Through a researcher-made evaluation tool, the stories' perceptive impact and relatability will be measured under a nonexperimental descriptive research design. Selected SHS students from Colegio de San Juan de Letran were given a literary selection (transposed to multiple versions with varying verb tenses and narrative viewpoints) and an adapted rating tool administered post-reading. Since the Shapiro-Wilk test of normality revealed that the data are not normally distributed, Mann–Whitney U tests were conducted to investigate the differences in literary perceptions by tense and point of view. Findings showed that all four variables exhibit no relationship across each other, indicating that readers perceive the time of a selection regardless of verb tense used and relate or not to the characters regardless of the story's narrative viewpoint. Contemporary Literature teachers and authors of literary works may then emphasize less the impact of verb tense and narrative viewpoint in both teaching and writing literature.

papers.title: Adaptability or Inadequacy: Lived Experiences of Out-of-Field English Teachers in Philippine Public High Schools
papers.abstract: Out-of-field (OOF) teaching, where teachers handle subjects outside their specialization, remains a persistent and systemic issue in Philippine public schools, particularly in English instruction. This study explored the lived experiences of eight non-English major high school teachers who were assigned to teach English despite their different academic preparation. Using online semi-structured interviews, the research examined their academic backgrounds, the challenges they encountered, the coping strategies they developed, and the types of support they received from their institutions.Thematic analysis revealed four key patterns: (1) limited language proficiency and insufficient content knowledge constrained effective classroom instruction and confidence; (2) teachers relied on adaptive strategies such as code-switching, self-study, and the use of digital resources to deliver lessons; (3) collegial support, mentoring, and division-led training partially mitigated instructional gaps, although access to these supports remained inconsistent across contexts; and (4) teachers expressed strong motivation and resilience but emphasized the urgent need for systemic reforms. These findings underscore the pressing need for regular, subject-specific training, structured mentorship programs, and improved deployment policies that better match teacher expertise with subject assignments. Strengthening institutional support systems is crucial to ease the burden on OOF teachers and to ensure more equitable, effective, and high-quality English language education in Philippine public schools.

papers.title: Hybrid Automated and Written Corrective Feedback (HAWCF) on the Argumentative Synthesis Writing of Grade 11 ESL Learners
papers.abstract: Developing ESL learners' argumentative synthesis writing, a genre that requires integrating information from multiple sources to support an argument, demands comprehensive feedback mechanisms. This study investigated the effect of combining Automated Corrective Feedback (ACF) and Written Corrective Feedback (WCF), termed Hybrid Automated and Written Corrective Feedback (HAWCF), on the argumentative synthesis writing of Grade 11 ESL learners, focusing on text quality, source use, and argumentation. Employing a convergent parallel mixed-methods design, the quantitative strand utilized a one-group pretest-posttest quasi-experimental design with a class of 30 Grade 11 learners, whose performance was evaluated using a researcher-made analytic rubric. The qualitative strand employed a phenomenological approach, with seven participants in semi-structured interviews. Paired-samples t-tests analyzed pretest and posttest differences, while Moustakas's steps of transcendental phenomenology guided qualitative interpretation. Findings revealed that HAWCF produced a statistically significant improvement from “Good Performance” to “Strong Performance” with a large effect size. Qualitative analysis revealed two themes: (1) View of HAWCF on Argumentative Synthesis Writing and (2) Processing of HAWCF on Argumentative Synthesis Writing. These themes describe the transformative shift in learners' views and processing, as they moved from initial overwhelm to active engagement and emergent writing autonomy. Data triangulation indicated that the observed improvements align with the learners' perceptions and cognitive, affective, and behavioral processing. Based on these findings, the study proposes a primer for implementing hybrid feedback in ESL classrooms titled “Synergizing Writing Feedback” that introduces the HAWCF and Writing Performance Interplay Model.

keynote.bio: Prof. Kuo-Sheng Cheng was born in Taipei, Taiwan. He received his B.Sc. and M.Sc. degrees in Electrical Engineering from National Cheng Kung University (NCKU), Tainan, Taiwan, in 1980 and 1982, respectively. He later earned an M.S. degree in Biomedical Engineering from Rensselaer Polytechnic Institute, Troy, NY, USA, in 1988, and a Ph.D. in Electrical Engineering from NCKU in 1990. Prof. Cheng has authored more than 150 papers in academic journals and conferences and has been invited as a keynote speaker at numerous international conferences.

papers.title: Demographic Profiles as Determinants of Self Efficacy and Self Management Behaviors of Diabetic Patients
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Introduction Self-management of diabetes involves individuals actively engaging in daily behaviors and decisions to effectively control blood glucose levels and prevent complications, which is crucial for improving quality of life and reducing the burden of the disease. Methodology This quantitative, cross-sectional study utilized the General Self-Efficacy Scale and Diabetes Self-Management Behavior Scale to assess the determinants of self-efficacy and management behaviors among diabetic patients. Findings Most of the diabetic patients are 60-69 years old, have diabetes for 1 to 5 years, no diabetes-related complications, have average literacy levels, and have access to digital health technologies. They have high level of self-efficacy for diabetes self-management in terms of behavioral self-efficacy, coping, and support utilization; high level of self-management behaviors in terms of diet and lifestyle; glucose monitoring and medication; risk prevention and complication management; information utilization & continuity of care engagement. There were no significant differences between the levels of self-efficacy for diabetes self-management when grouped according to age, gender, duration of diabetes, presence of diabetes-related complications, literacy levels and access to digital health technologies; no significant differences between the levels of diabetes self-management behaviors when grouped according to age, gender, duration of illness, literacy levels, but with significant differences as to the category Glucose Monitoring and Medication when grouped according to presence of diabetes-related complications; as to the categories: Glucose Monitoring and Medication; Information Utilization & Continuity of Care Engagement; and Level of Diabetes Self-Management Behaviors, when grouped according to access to digital health technologies. Conclusion The study concludes that diabetic patients generally exhibit high self-efficacy and self-management behaviors regardless of demographic factors, with access to digital health technologies significantly enhancing specific aspects of their diabetes care.

papers.title: Patient's profile Satisfaction and Experience with Diabetes Self Management support System (PSE-DMSS)
papers.abstract: Abstract Introduction Diabetes self-management support systems play a vital role in enhancing patient outcomes by promoting continuity of care, interdisciplinary collaboration, and patient engagement. Understanding patient satisfaction and experiences with these systems is essential in improving care delivery and ensuring effective long-term disease management. Methods This study employed a quantitative, cross-sectional design to evaluate the extent of patient satisfaction and experience with the Diabetes Self-Management Support System (PSE-DMSS). Measures focused on four key domains: perceived continuity of care, interdisciplinary collaboration experience, nurse-led support, and system experience. Statistical analyses, including independent t-tests and one-way ANOVA, were conducted to determine differences in satisfaction levels across demographic and clinical variables such as age, gender, duration of diabetes, presence of complications, health literacy, and access to digital health technologies. Findings Results showed a high level of patient satisfaction and experience across all PSE-DMSS domains, with mean scores ranging from 3.45 to 3.54, indicating consistently positive perceptions of care delivery. No significant differences were found when satisfaction levels were grouped according to age, gender, presence of diabetes-related complications, health literacy, and access to digital health technologies. However, significant differences were observed when grouped according to duration of diabetes, particularly in interdisciplinary collaboration, nurse-led support, system experience, and overall satisfaction, suggesting that patient experience evolves with disease duration. Conclusion The findings of this study support the SDG#3 Health and Wellbeing as it indicates that patients generally report high satisfaction and positive experiences with the PSE-DMSS, underscoring its effectiveness as a support mechanism in diabetes care. While most demographic and clinical factors did not significantly influence satisfaction, duration of diabetes emerged as an important determinant. These results highlight the need for tailored interventions that consider patients' length of illness to further improve support systems and optimize care outcomes.

papers.title: Beyond Borders: Intercultural Teaching Experiences of English Pre-service Teachers in an International Practicum Immersion
papers.abstract: The internationalization of teacher education has created opportunities for pre-service teachers in fostering intercultural competence and pedagogical development beyond borders. The study aimed to explore the lived experiences of English pre-service teachers during their practicum immersion abroad and how these experiences shaped their teaching perspectives and practices, program implementation gaps, and provided insights for improved international practicum experiences. The researchers employed descriptive qualitative research design. Through purposive sampling, a total of six participants, five pre-service teachers and one in-service teacher who had participated in the program the preceding year, were asked to describe their experiences through online semi-structured interviews and reflective questionnaires. The findings revealed key experiences, including adapting language barriers, cultural adaptations and challenges, and implementing teaching strategy modifications. The participants also gained a deeper understanding of multilingual education and reported an increase in their confidence and flexibility in their teaching approaches. The value of international immersion was also emphasized in preparing future teachers for multicultural classrooms and global education contexts, where intercultural understanding and pedagogical adaptability are essential. The study recommends strengthening international practicum programs through comprehensive pre-departure orientations, sustained supervisory support, and extended immersion durations to better equip pre-service teachers for intercultural teaching and professional growth.

papers.title: Resilience in Transition: Adversity Quotient and Coping Strategies of First-Year Education Students
papers.abstract: The transition to higher education is a critical stage where students encounter academic, social, and personal challenges. In disaster-prone contexts such as Cavite State University Naic Campus, these challenges are compounded by recurring natural phenomena including extreme heat index, flooding, and earthquakes that often disrupt classes and force sudden shifts to flexible learning modalities. This study investigated the resilience of first-year education students by examining their Adversity Quotient (AQ) and coping strategies, analyzed within a gendered lens. A mixed-methods sequential explanatory design was employed. Quantitative data were collected using Stoltz's Adversity Response Profile® and Carver's Brief COPE Questionnaire, while qualitative interviews provided contextual insights into students' experiences of adapting to flexible learning during environmental emergencies. Findings revealed that most respondents fell within low (48.18%) and moderate (48.18%) AQ categories in terms of control, with only 3.64% reaching high AQ. Ownership emerged as a relative strength, with 21.81% in the high category, while reach remained weak (54.55% low). Endurance showed promise, with 30.91% attaining high AQ. Gender differences in AQ were negligible (t \= 0.623, p \= 0.534). In coping strategies, problem-focused coping was most prevalent (59.09%, M \= 3.09), followed by emotion-focused coping (27.27%, M \= 2.92), while avoidance coping was least preferred (13.64%, M \= 2.40). A significant gender difference was observed only in emotion-focused coping (p \= 0.002). Correlation analysis indicated strong positive relationships between AQ and both problem-focused (r \= 0.56) and emotion-focused coping (r \= 0.56), with a moderate positive relationship for avoidance coping (r \= 0.32). The study concludes that resilience is a multifaceted construct shaped by AQ dimensions and constructive coping strategies. In contexts of environmental disruption, resilience-building programs and inclusive student support services are essential to sustain learning continuity and strengthen adaptation among first-year education students.

papers.title: Silent Crisis: Work Engagement, Organizational Justice, and Commitment in Philippine Education
papers.abstract: In line with the recent investigations into the lack of transparency and inconsistent decision-making among administrators in the Philippine educational system, this study investigates the mediating role of work engagement in the relationship between perceived procedural and informational justice and affective commitment among employees in selected educational institutions in the Philippines. The study employed a quantitative research design gathering data from 306 respondents across 6 educational institutions through an online survey reviewed and validated by subject-matter experts. The findings show that work engagement significantly mediates the relationship between the perceived procedural and informational justice and affective commitment. These findings contribute to addressing the contextual gap based on industry (education), enhancing the understanding of organizational justice within the post-pandemic landscape. Grounded in the theories of procedural and informational justice, the Job Demands–Resources model, and Social Exchange Theory, this study offers theoretical and practical insights for policy development and institutional practice. Future research may extend these findings by employing more complex models and alternative methodological or philosophical approaches, such as post-positivism or critical realism.

papers.title: Faith, Food, Family: Investigating a Filipino Enclave in South Korea
papers.abstract: The present study employs autoethnographic research to explore Little Manila in Hyehwadong, Seoul, South Korea. As an informal Filipino community located in the capital city, the proponent of the study draws on personal reflections and immersive engagements to capture the narratives of Filipino migrants as they build their communities through identity formation and social structures while being in a foreign land. Socio-cultural dynamics have shaped the transnational space through emerging challenges and experiences faced by Filipinos who have left the Philippines for various reasons. The autoethnographic experience highlights three prominent faces: the space (Little Manila at the End of the Tunnel), the tastes and flavors (Food at the Core of Filipino Gatherings Overseas), and the spirituality (Catholicism and Sundays as Little Manila's Defining Experience). As a vital hub central to cultural preservation, harmonious coexistence, and identity formation, Little Manila also emerges as a space for community support, offering a sense of belonging and familiarity in a foreign country. Ultimately, this study aims to provide insights into the lives of Filipinos in South Korea and contribute to the discussion on Filipino identity, migration, and community support in the contemporary landscape.

speakers.label: PLENARY SPEAKER 1
speakers.name: Dr. Hsiao-Yeh CHU
speakers.title: AI-Enabled Smart Manufacturing Education: Sustainability, Inclusive Innovation, and Global Talent Development
speakers.bio: Dr. Hsiao-Yeh (Mike) Chu is a Professor in the Department of Mechanical Engineering and Director of the Micro-Precision Manufacturing Center at Kun Shan University, Taiwan. He holds a Ph.D. in Mechanical Engineering from National Cheng Kung University. His research spans tribology, lubrication engineering, machine condition monitoring, and AI applications in smart manufacturing. He has led government-funded and industry-sponsored projects and contributed to technology transfer in machine lubrication, sensing, and manufacturing process improvement. His publications address vibration-based predictive maintenance, online quality monitoring in injection molding, and CNC tool-wear classification using spindle motor current. Dr. Chu also serves as Chief Executive Officer of the Taiwan-Philippines INTACT Base Office, supporting the INTENSE Program and educational collaboration between Taiwan and the Philippines. Through his work with international students and industry partners, he connects research training with practical engineering challenges. His academic and international engagement brings together applied research, industry-oriented education, and talent development, with an emphasis on expanding opportunities for students to pursue advanced study and gain industrial experience.
speakers.abstract: This plenary presentation examines how AI-enabled smart manufacturing can support engineering education that connects sustainability with inclusive innovation and global talent development. Drawing on research and university-industry collaboration at Kun Shan University, it links manufacturing problems with opportunities for student learning and international cooperation. Research examples include vibration-based lubrication monitoring, predictive maintenance of forming machinery, online quality monitoring in injection molding, and CNC tool-condition classification using spindle motor current. In a published CNC milling study, a model combining spectral features, principal component analysis, and logistic regression achieved 97.44% accuracy on held-out signal windows under fixed machining conditions. This finding illustrates both the potential of accessible sensing and the importance of validating AI models within their intended operating conditions. Ongoing research on command-synchronized current monitoring further highlights the challenges of industrial application. Using these cases, the presentation proposes a learning approach that connects mechanical principles with data acquisition, feature interpretation, model evaluation, and engineering decisions. It discusses how better-informed maintenance and process decisions may support sustainability by reducing unnecessary tool replacement, lubricant use, and production waste. The presentation also draws on international research training and the INTENSE Program to examine pathways linking advanced study, industry experience, and career development. It considers how university partnerships, mentoring, and participation in practical research can widen access to engineering opportunities. The discussion identifies requirements for connecting AI competencies with engineering judgment and international collaboration, while recognizing the need to evaluate educational outcomes and sustainability benefits in practice.

speakers.title: Shaping Resilient Institutions: Connecting Knowledge, Technology, and People
speakers.bio:
She is a graduate of Ateneo de Manila University with a degree in BS Management and currently serves as the Head of Product Marketing and Customer Success (PMCS) at CE-Logic, Inc.

She leads the team responsible for developing product-focused marketing, implementation, training, and customer engagement initiatives for CE-Logic's partner institutions. Through PMCS, she works to bridge the gap between providing access to academic resources and ensuring their meaningful adoption—helping institutions maximize their investments in digital solutions and achieve their desired outcomes in teaching, learning, and research.

Her work is particularly relevant as Philippine higher education continues to advance digital transformation, research and innovation, and the development of future-ready learning ecosystems. In this evolving landscape, she advocates for a customer success approach that goes beyond implementation by fostering sustained product adoption, meaningful engagement, and long-term institutional value.

Through her leadership of PMCS, Daniella works closely with higher education institutions to help ensure that technology and academic resources translate into measurable impact for their faculty, researchers, students, and the broader academic community.
speakers.abstract: As AI reshapes education and research, institutional resilience depends not only on technology but also on access to trusted knowledge, capable people, and sustainable systems. This session explores how institutions can build an inclusive research and learning ecosystem through digital solutions, quality information resources, capacity-building programs, and strategic partnerships. It will also highlight CE-Logic's role in connecting institutions with solutions and support that advance their academic, research, and innovation goals.

speakers.label: PLENARY SPEAKER 3
speakers.name: Dr. Ricardo BAGARINAO
speakers.title: A Double-Edged Transformation: The Paradox of AI and Sustainability in Education
speakers.bio: He has built a career that brings together teaching, academic leadership, environmental research, and the evolving field of open and digital learning. He joined the University of the Philippines Open University (UPOU) as a full-time faculty member in 2006, where he taught biology and related courses in the Faculty of Education and the Faculty of Management and Development Studies. His years at UPOU have taken him through various academic and administrative roles. He served as Program Chair of the PhD in Education, University Registrar, Dean of the Faculty of Education, and Director of the Center for Open and Digital Teaching and Learning. He currently serves as Assistant to the Chancellor for Sustainability and the Program Chair of the Doctor in Sustainability. His research interests reflect a continuing concern for the relationship between people, places, and the environment. These include landscape ecology, land use and land cover change, environmental management, disaster preparedness and risk reduction, and spatial analysis using geographic information systems. His work in open and distance education has likewise expanded his research into e-learning and open learning. He has published in peer-reviewed and indexed national and international journals and contributed chapters to books published locally and internationally. Behind these credentials is an academic journey that has moved across disciplines and institutions—from biology and environmental research to education, digital learning, and sustainability.
speakers.abstract: Education shapes sustainability direction while artificial intelligence (AI) rapidly transforms education and re-shapes knowledge creation, access, sharing, and application. Though AI offers new opportunities for more inclusive and sustainable education, it also operates with growing concerns about energy and resource consumption, environmental impacts, privacy, unequal access, and social inequality. The paper examines this double-edged transformation, challenging the assumption that technological innovation is always progressive or sustainable. It also explores how educators and institutions can navigate the tensions between innovation and responsibility, efficiency and ecological cost, personalization and privacy, access and inequality, and technological capability and human judgment. More importantly, it positions education not simply as a user of AI, but as a force that can shape how societies understand, govern, and use AI. The paper concludes that sustainable use of AI in education must go beyond technological adoption. It requires critical AI literacy, ethical responsibility, ecological awareness, and informed human judgment to ensure that AI contributes to more inclusive, responsible, and sustainable futures.

speakers.label: PLENARY SPEAKER 4
speakers.name: Dr. Mohd Erfino JOHARI
speakers.title: Human-Centred AI in Higher Education: From Intelligent Technology to Ethical, Inclusive and Future-Ready Universities
speakers.bio:
Dr. Mohd Erfino Johari is a Malaysian academic leader with over 30 years of experience in higher education governance, international academic diplomacy, public service, and corporate leadership. He currently serves as Deputy Vice-Chancellor (Academic and Internationalisation) at Universiti Poly-Tech Malaysia (UPTM), where he leads academic transformation, global partnerships, dual-degree initiatives and institutional internationalisation strategies. He previously served as Director of Industrial Linkages and Academic Internationalisation (ILAI) and contributes actively to university governance through Senate committees and scholarly editorial boards.

His career spans significant roles within the Malaysian Ministry of Education and the Ministry of Higher Education, including service as Education Attaché for Malaysia in the United Kingdom and Ireland and later as Director & Counsellor (Education) at the Malaysian High Commission in New Zealand, advancing bilateral academic cooperation and cross-border education initiatives. He also held senior corporate leadership roles as Chief Corporate Officer and Acting Chief Marketing Officer, contributing expertise in strategic governance, institutional branding and organisational performance.

Internationally engaged, he serves as Visiting Professor/Lecturer at Universidad De Ixtlahuaca Mexico, Universitas PGRI Indonesia, Universitas Nahdlatul Ulama Indonesia and Universitas Ahmad Dahlan Indonesia. Appointed as International Research Fellow at Shinawatra International University Thailand and the International Cultural Communication Center Malaysia (ICCCM). He was invited as Keynote Speaker at SCTE2025 in Cairo, Egypt. He currently holds ten research grants including the FRGS (MOHE) and published more than 20 indexed journal articles for the last 3 years across Scopus, Web of Science, ERA, and MyCite. His research has earned Best Paper Awards at ICAR2023 and ICAR2025, as well as the Best Presenter Award at ICAR2025. He holds a PhD from UPSI in Education, a Master's degree from OUM, and a Bachelor's degree from University of Jordan, with additional qualifications in education, management and counselling. His research focuses on Geo-Islamica education, Shariah-compliant governance, higher education policy, internationalisation strategy and nation-building. Guided by principles of integrity, inclusivity, and service, he continues to advance globally connected universities and future-ready graduates through scholarship, diplomacy, and strategic academic leadership.
speakers.abstract: As Artificial Intelligence (AI) rapidly redefines the global educational landscape, higher education institutions stand at a critical crossroads. The mandate facing academic leaders is no longer merely adopting intelligent technologies, but strategically steering them to serve human flourishing, educational equity and institutional resilience. This keynote outlines a comprehensive framework for embedding Human-Centred AI (HCAI) across university ecosystems by integrating the universal ethical principles of Maqasid Shariah (the higher objectives of Islamic law). By translating these profound objectives, the preservation of values, human dignity, intellect, future generations and equitable resources, into a modern techno-academic context, the presentation offers a robust philosophical and practical model for AI governance. Drawing from strategic initiatives at Universiti Poly-Tech Malaysia (UPTM), the session addresses five interconnected pillars: ethical governance, authentic assessment, inclusive pedagogy, responsible innovation and sustainable institutional transformation. Ultimately, this presentation advocates for a balanced academic ecosystem where intelligent technology and human wisdom co-exist to prepare ethical leaders for an automated world.
